summary: This informational document examines how existing IP mobility protocols are deployed in distributed mobility management environments. It then identifies where they fall short compared with the requirements set for a distributed mobility solution.

eli5.summary: When your phone moves, the network must keep your connection going. This note checks whether today's tricks work when the helpers are spread around, and lists where they do not.

subtitle: How today's mobility protocols work when anchors are distributed instead of centralized.

tldr.problem: Current IP mobility management protocols (Mobile IPv6, Proxy Mobile IPv6) were designed with centralized mobility anchors that manage traffic for millions of users. This creates bottlenecks and suboptimal routing, especially in flat wireless and 3GPP networks trying to distribute mobility functions.
tldr.mechanism: This document analyzes how distributed mobility management (DMM) can be achieved using existing mobility protocols by deploying multiple anchors, distributing anchoring functions, and selecting optimal anchors at attachment or dynamically. It examines practices in host-based (Mobile IPv6, NEMO), network-based (Proxy Mobile IPv6), and 3GPP systems, and identifies where they fall short of DMM requirements.
tldr.outcome: The gap analysis reveals that while protocols can be deployed distributedly, significant limitations remain: no dynamic anchor switching during sessions, no efficient anchor discovery, lack of per-session mobility control, and incomplete separation of control and data planes. These gaps guide future protocol extensions.

facts.label: Main gap
facts.value: No dynamic anchor change during sessions

today: RFC 7429 remains an Informational document providing gap analysis based on RFC 7333 requirements. It is not itself updated or obsoleted. The gaps it identifies continue to guide distributed mobility management research and development. Some gaps have been partially addressed through RFC 6463 (runtime LMA assignment), RFC 7389 (control-plane/user-plane separation), and other extensions, but comprehensive DMM solutions typically require new protocol designs beyond simple extensions of existing protocols.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Distributed Mobility Management (DMM) is an approach to handling mobile node (MN) connectivity when devices move between networks. Existing mobility protocols like Mobile IPv6 (MIPv6) and Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) use a single centralized mobility anchor (Home Agent or Local Mobility Anchor) to manage the traffic of all mobile nodes in an operator's network.

This centralized design creates problems: traffic from a mobile node must traverse the anchor even when the destination is nearby, creating suboptimal routing; the anchor becomes a single point of failure and a scaling bottleneck for millions of users. Distributed mobility management proposes spreading the anchor function across the network, with different sessions anchored at different points.

This informational document investigates whether today's IP mobility protocols can be deployed to provide distributed mobility management. It describes current practices in IP wireless networks and 3GPP mobile networks and identifies the limitations in these practices compared to the DMM requirements defined in RFC 7333.
sections.eli5: When your phone moves to a new network, someone needs to keep track of you so messages still reach you. Right now, one person does this for everyone, which slows things down. This document explores whether many people can share the job and points out what does not work yet.

sections.title: Mobility Management Functions
sections.content:
The main mobility management functions of existing protocols are three: The Anchoring Function (AF) allocates an IP address or prefix (Home Address or Home Network Prefix) to a mobile node and advertises it to the routing infrastructure; the Location Management (LM) function keeps track of where the mobile node is currently attached (its Care-of Address) and maintains a binding between its home address and its current location; and the Forwarding Management (FM) function intercepts and forwards packets to or from the mobile node based on location information, typically using tunnels.

In Mobile IPv6, the home agent provides anchoring and location management server functions, the mobile node has the location management client function, and tunneling is split between them. In Proxy Mobile IPv6, the local mobility anchor provides anchoring and location management server functions, the mobile access gateway provides location management client and FM functions. In Hierarchical Mobile IPv6, the Mobility Anchor Point serves as an intermediate aggregator between the home agent and the mobile node. Distributing these functions means deploying multiple anchors that can each serve different sessions of the same mobile node.
sections.eli5: Three jobs must happen: giving you a home address, keeping track of where you are, and moving messages to and from you. Spreading these jobs means different servers can do them for different things you are doing on your phone.

sections.title: DMM Deployment Practices
sections.content:
Host-based approaches like Mobile IPv6 and NEMO can be distributed by deploying several Home Agents and assigning the topologically closest one to each mobile node. Mobile IPv6 Route Optimization (RO) allows the mobile node to communicate directly with correspondent nodes using its current Care-of Address, reducing traffic through the home agent. However, RO requires signaling overhead, support from correspondent nodes, and is unavailable for NEMO.

Hierarchical Mobile IPv6 introduces a Mobility Anchor Point closer to the mobile node, reducing signaling and improving handover performance. Multiple MAPs in a local domain enable distributed operation with flexible MAP selection based on expected mobility patterns or topological distance.

Network-based Proxy Mobile IPv6 can be decentralized by deploying multiple Local Mobility Anchors with static or dynamic selection of which LMA serves which mobile node. Local Routing Extensions enable optimal routing between mobile nodes attached to the same or different MAGs but the same LMA. Runtime LMA Assignment specifies a mechanism for changing the assigned LMA during mobility, enabling load balancing and optimal anchor selection.

3GPP networks use the Packet Data Network Gateway (P-GW) as a centralized anchor, similar to PMIPv6. Local IP Access (LIPA) and Selected IP Traffic Offload (SIPTO) enable offloading some IP services without traversing the core network, though with limited mobility support. The 3GPP architecture provides gateway discovery and selection mechanisms based on topological location.
sections.eli5: Existing systems can spread anchors by putting many servers in the network, picking the closest one, or moving to a better one. Some tricks like direct routing between users or local gateways help, but they do not work everywhere.

sections.title: Identified Gaps
sections.content:
The analysis identifies critical gaps preventing full DMM deployment: GAP1-1 is the lack of dynamic anchor change during ongoing sessions; existing protocols support only initial anchor assignment. GAP1-2 is that mobile nodes managing multiple anchors lack mechanisms to intelligently select source addresses per session or to know anchor properties. GAP1-3 is the absence of efficient anchor discovery and selection mechanisms; DHAAD, the home agent flag in Router Advertisements, and 3GPP gateway discovery could help. GAP1-4 is incomplete separation of control-plane and data-plane forwarding management; distributing only the data plane while keeping centralized control creates challenges.

GAP2-1 is that applications do not signal whether they need per-session mobility support, and the network lacks mechanisms to correlate sessions with anchors. GAP2-2 is that mobile nodes lack knowledge of assigned IP address properties (whether they provide mobility support). GAP2-3 is inadequate session identification granularity; protocols identify users and devices but not individual application sessions.

Additional gaps include incomplete operation and management support, undefined means for testing and monitoring DMM deployment, and limited multicast support due to tunnel convergence problems.
sections.eli5: The main problems are: you cannot switch to a better anchor while talking, the phone does not know which address is safe to use for which app, there is no easy way to find available anchors, and control commands stay central even when data spreads out.

sections.title: Requirements Not Met
sections.content:
RFC 7333 specifies eight DMM requirements. Requirement REQ1 (Distributed mobility management) requires avoiding suboptimal routing by supporting multiple anchors and dynamic anchor selection; current protocols support multiple anchors but lack dynamic switching. REQ2 (Bypassable mobility per session) requires choosing whether to use mobility for each application session; protocols lack per-session control and address property exposure. REQ3 (IPv6 deployment) is generally met by existing protocols.

REQ4 (Reuse existing protocols) is the motivation for this analysis; while distribution is possible, the gaps prevent full compliance. REQ5 (Coexistence) is met; DMM practices coexist with legacy deployments. REQ6 (Operations and management) lacks standardized configuration with NETCONF/YANG and thorough documentation. REQ7 (Security) is not newly compromised by distribution, though security associations must be managed across multiple anchors. REQ8 (Multicast) is poorly addressed; tunnel convergence problems remain unsolved in DMM contexts.
sections.eli5: Most of the rules from the main requirements document are not fully met by today's systems. The main problems are switching anchors mid-conversation, choosing per-app whether to use mobility, and managing many anchor points safely.
